new_texts: The words of the narration, written out and checked before anyone records them.
Walker stands at the edge of the first gap.
He jumps, and the camera follows him across the whole gap without cutting away.
The spike kills him, and he restarts at the last checkpoint in under a second.
He reaches the flag, the level ends, and the game offers a restart, which we show now.
The script is the narration, written under each frame so it can be counted and cut.

slides.source: Source: godot-waikthrough SKILL.md and capture-and-coverage.md; Chapter 0, headless runs and --fixed-fps; glossary, Toolchain.

new_texts: Computing each frame offline, as slowly as needed, then joining the frames into a film.
OFFLINE RENDER: 10 S FILM AT 30 FPS
120 times slower than the film plays (4 s a frame is illustrative)
Slow is fine: nobody watches a render run. It is not a frame-rate test.
Render builds every frame offline, so quality can beat speed. It proves nothing about live fps.

new_texts: How many frames are shown each second.

all_texts: How many frames are shown each second.

new_texts: Frame rate times duration: how many frames the film needs.
Every frame is stored or rendered. 60 fps doubles the work of 30.
Frame count is rate × duration: 30 fps for 10 s is 300 frames.

slides.title: Before you show a walkthrough film

slides.picture: A checklist of six items drawn one at a time.

new_texts: Does every shot serve the one-sentence idea?
Does the film say what it is not in its first two beats?
Was the route measured: speed, turn rate, height?
Is every clip real capture, or labelled constructed?
Do the words fit each beat and the sound fit its window?
Does every claim in the narration have evidence on screen?
Then say it exactly: not “make it smoother”, but “1.25 m/s, linear, under 1.5”.
